title: If multi-agent learning is the answer, what is the question?
read: Start with Section 5, then return to the examples that motivate its five research agendas.
note: A useful first reading because success depends on the question: computing a solution, explaining observed learning, identifying equilibrium learning rules, or designing an agent for a particular setting. Use these distinctions throughout the collection. The paper’s technical use of “normative” is narrower than the later collection on normative agency.
question: What kind of claim would count as success for each of today’s perspectives?

title: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
read: Read the taxonomy first; choose one failure mode and one risk factor to follow in detail.
note: Organizes multi-agent risks around miscoordination, conflict, and collusion, with factors such as commitment problems and destabilising dynamics cutting across them. Use it to connect the day’s formal models to safety questions. Coordination can help the participating agents while harming people outside their coalition.
question: Who benefits from an apparent improvement in cooperation, and who is left out of the model?

title: Open Challenges in Multi-Agent Security
authors: Schroeder de Witt, Krawiecka, Krawczuk et al.
read: Read the threat-model overview and select the challenges closest to monitoring or agent communication.
note: Broadens the safety discussion to interacting agents, their communication, and the infrastructure around them. Pair it with the control collection: a protocol can only be evaluated against the channels and adversaries its model includes. Treat the proposed challenges as a research agenda, rather than evidence that every listed failure is equally likely.
question: Which trust boundary changes when an individually evaluated model becomes part of a larger system?

title: Cooperative and uncooperative institution designs
read: Begin with the program-game setup and illustrative institutions; save the full technical development for a second pass.
note: Shows why inspecting another agent’s operating procedure can change the strategic problem. Conditional commitments support surprising cooperative and uncooperative outcomes. Track what each program can observe and prove, and distinguish an equilibrium between program designers from a best response in the original action game.
question: What changes when the strategic choice is a program rather than an action?

title: Robust Cooperation in the Prisoner’s Dilemma: Program Equilibrium via Provability Logic
read: Read the modal-agent construction alongside the FairBot slides; inspect the updated caveat on bounded analogues.
note: The formal route from mutual source access to robust cooperation through provability logic. Keep the idealized mathematical agent separate from a finite procedure with a proof-search budget. The 2021 update explicitly cautions that bounded analogues of these results had not been proved there; an unbounded argument does not supply a runtime guarantee.
question: Which part of the cooperation argument fails to follow merely from giving a program a finite search budget?

title: Robust program equilibrium
read: Follow the simulation-based construction and its grounding mechanism before comparing equilibrium guarantees.
note: A complementary route to program equilibrium, using simulations of the other program rather than the same proof machinery as modal agents. Work through why recursion needs grounding and how the resulting construction treats opponents. Compare its assumptions and attainable outcomes with the later simulation-based characterization.
question: What makes recursive simulation terminate, and what does that mechanism cost strategically?

title: Similarity-based cooperative equilibrium
read: Read the similarity-game definition and one learning experiment.
note: Studies a setting where agents observe a similarity signal instead of complete source code. The paper separates equilibrium possibilities from experiments in which cooperation is learned. Read the assumptions on that signal closely: a theorem about a specified similarity game does not establish that an arbitrary measure of neural-network similarity provides the required incentives.
question: Which properties must the similarity signal have for the strategic argument to apply?

title: Characterising Simulation-Based Program Equilibria
read: Compare the statements with and without shared randomness before entering the proofs.
note: Extends simulation-based program constructions and characterizes which equilibrium outcomes they can support. Shared randomness makes a substantive difference, and the paper identifies limits without it. Read this after Oesterheld: it helps distinguish a convenient example of cooperation from a characterization of a whole family of program equilibria.
question: Where does the availability of shared randomness enter the achievable-outcome claim?

title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning: Foundations and Modern Approaches
read: Use Chapters 3–5 selectively for stochastic games, solution concepts, and the challenges of simultaneous learning.
note: The reference to open when the dynamics talk assumes unfamiliar game or reinforcement-learning vocabulary. Separate the environment state, each agent’s policy, and the learning rule that changes that policy. The estimated time covers selected sections, not the whole book; the author site provides a freely accessible PDF and accompanying code.
question: What is stationary from one learner’s perspective when the other learners are also updating?

title: A Pair-Approximation Method for Modelling the Dynamics of Multi-Agent Stochastic Games
read: Focus on the stochastic-game assumptions, pair variables, and comparison with agent-based simulations.
note: Develops a pair-approximation model of myopic Q-learning with symmetric state transitions. The important move is to retain local pair information while closing the hierarchy of higher-order dependencies. Ask what the approximation captures beyond a population average, and which graph structures or correlations could undermine it.
question: Which correlations are represented explicitly, and which are supplied by the closure assumption?

title: Emergent Fast-Slow Dynamics in Multi-Agent Q-Learning for Networked Stochastic Games
read: Read after Chu et al.; track the small-learning-rate assumption and the simulation comparisons.
note: Extends the dynamics picture by separating rapid state transitions from slower Q-value evolution. The resulting approximation uses stationary state distributions for the slowly changing learning variables. Check both timescales: a small update step alone is not a blanket guarantee that every relevant state process mixes quickly enough.
question: How would you detect that the fast process has stopped equilibrating before the slow variables move appreciably?

title: Multiagent Learning: Foundations and Recent Trends
read: Use the tutorial selectively to revisit game models and the families of learning approaches.
note: A slide-based companion when you want another route into the foundational concepts. Read it alongside the newer textbook rather than as a survey of developments after 2017. Compare what an algorithm is designed to achieve with the dynamics its interaction actually produces.
question: Is the learning rule meant to find an equilibrium, adapt to an opponent, or optimize a common objective?

title: AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion
read: Start with the deployment setup, safety and usefulness metrics, and trusted versus untrusted monitoring.
note: Evaluates protocols for using a capable model while assuming that it might intentionally subvert the task. Read the programming-assistant experiments together with their threat model. The result concerns the tested protocol and attacks; it does not demonstrate that the underlying model has benign goals or that an untested deployment is safe.
question: What can the attacker observe, choose, and coordinate, and which of those powers does the evaluation cover?

title: When can we trust untrusted monitoring? A safety case sketch across collusion strategies
read: Read the safety-case sketch, then Appendix D’s collusion taxonomy; use Appendix B for the mathematics.
note: The closest reading companion to Morgan Sinclaire’s talk. Distinguishes passive self-recognition, causal and acausal collusion, and combined strategies, while making assumptions and remaining challenges explicit. Compare measuring a monitor’s discrimination on test data with bounding collusion opportunities across a deployment.
question: Which collusion strategy could succeed without an explicit message from the acting model?

title: Games for AI Control: Models of Safety Evaluations of AI Deployment Protocols
read: Trace the formal game components back to the protocol-designer and adversary roles.
note: Models control evaluations as partially observable stochastic games with safety and usefulness objectives. It makes choices about information, strategy spaces, and evaluation procedures explicit. Use the formalism to examine the assumptions behind a reported score, including how the tested adversary relates to possible deployment attacks.
question: What changes in the game if the adversary can select when to attack?

title: Safety Cases: How to Justify the Safety of Advanced AI Systems
read: Read the framework and compare a control argument with an argument based on trustworthiness.
note: Explains how multiple pieces of evidence can support a structured safety argument. Its distinction between inability, control, trustworthiness, and deference helps locate what a control evaluation contributes. Write down the assumptions joining the evidence to the conclusion, especially where several pieces depend on the same untested premise.
question: Which premise, if false, would defeat several apparently separate lines of evidence?

title: Lessons from Recent Multi-Agent Safety Incidents
read: Read as a synthesis, then follow the cited incident reports in Collection VI.
note: Draws lessons about composition, correlated failures, and the tension between useful cooperation and harmful collusion. Use it to generate questions for the primary reports. Keep a proposed general lesson separate from what a particular observed incident establishes about other models, tasks, or deployments.
question: Which suggested failure would be missed by evaluating each agent in isolation?

title: Empirical Game-Theoretic Analysis: A Survey
read: Begin with the EGTA process, then choose payoff estimation and strategy exploration as your two technical threads.
note: The anchor for the afternoon’s computational perspective: construct a finite game from simulation, analyze it, and search for missing strategies. Keep sampling uncertainty separate from the restriction to a policy set. This survey is cited in the supplied lecture and worksheet; it supplements the schedule’s 42-item bibliography.
question: Does a small regret estimate certify the underlying interaction, or only the strategies represented in the empirical game?

title: A Unified Game-Theoretic Approach to Multiagent Reinforcement Learning
read: Follow the PSRO loop: population, empirical payoffs, meta-strategy, and approximate response oracle.
note: Connects empirical games to learning new policies against mixtures of existing policies. The paper also examines overfitting to training partners through joint-policy correlation. Distinguish a learned approximate response from an exact best response; failure to discover a profitable deviation does not by itself prove that none exists.
question: Which parts of the stopping argument would require an exact oracle or a certified approximation?

title: The separation principle: where do beliefs and desires come from?
read: Read the inference–control argument, then test its interpretation against the POMDP and control references below.
note: A conceptual entry to representing agency through beliefs and goals using results from control and reinforcement learning. Distinguish the existence of an optimal policy using a sufficient belief state from a claim that an observed system explicitly implements separate belief and desire modules. General POMDP planning also allows actions to influence future information.
question: What would need to be observed to turn a useful representation of an optimal policy into a claim about implementation?

title: Planning and acting in partially observable stochastic domains
read: Focus on the belief-state formulation and how planning operates over distributions on hidden states.
note: Provides the technical grounding for the belief-state view. Under the model’s assumptions, a posterior over the current hidden state can summarize the history relevant to future decision-making. This does not reduce general partially observed control to choosing the action that would be best at a single estimated state.
question: When can two histories with the same current belief be treated identically for future planning?

title: Optimal control of Markov processes with incomplete state information
read: Use as a historical mathematical reference for incomplete-state-information control.
note: Follow how the hidden-state problem is reformulated in terms of available information. Read with the POMDP survey for context and notation. Keep the formal state and observation assumptions visible when relating the construction to modern learning systems; a theorem about an optimal controller does not automatically identify a trained model’s internal algorithm.
question: Which model assumptions make the information state sufficient?

title: The Separation Principle in Stochastic Control, Redux
read: Focus on the conditions for separation and the treatment of admissible feedback laws.
note: A technical corrective to overly broad appeals to the separation principle. Even familiar stochastic-control settings contain subtleties about how feedback systems are defined. Compare its precise theorem with the broader conceptual claim that agency involves inference and control, and distinguish classical separation from general belief-state planning.
question: Which conclusion is specific to the theorem’s control setting, rather than a universal property of agents?

title: Bayesian Filtering and Smoothing
read: Select the Bayesian filtering recursion and an example; treat the rest as a reference.
note: Supplies the inference machinery behind the belief-state discussion. Filtering estimates a present state from observations so far; smoothing can use later observations to estimate an earlier state. Keep those information sets distinct when explaining what an agent could know at the time of a decision.
question: Does the proposed explanation give the agent access to observations that arrive only after it acts?

title: Utilities as Legendre duals of probabilities
read: Read after the separation essay; focus on the definition of achievable distributions and its dual description.
note: Explores how the distributions an agent can bring about admit a description in terms of utilities through convex duality. The construction invites a different view of capability. Distinguish describing a set of attainable outcomes from identifying the objective an agent actually pursues within that set.
question: What can a dual description tell you about capability without telling you which outcome the agent prefers?

title: Elements of Information Theory
read: Consult entropy, mutual information, and source–channel separation as needed; this is not a cover-to-cover assignment.
note: Background for both the separation discussion and later readings on emergence and individuality. The study-time rating is for a selected topic. Match each information-theoretic quantity to its variables and distribution before interpreting it as evidence about goals, representation, or causal organization.
question: What does the measured information quantify, and what additional argument would connect it to agency?

title: Discovering agents
read: Read the causal definition of agency and a worked example before the discovery procedure.
note: Defines agents in terms of how their policies would adapt when the causal influence of their actions changes. This puts pressure on assumptions that simply label a subsystem an agent. Consider the required interventions and modeling assumptions before applying the discovery claim to passive behavioral observations.
question: Which policy changes would count as evidence of agency under this definition?

title: Transformers learn factored representations
read: Compare product and factored representations, then inspect the synthetic data-generating processes.
note: Tests predictions about the geometry of transformer representations using processes with known latent structure. Factoring trades dimensional efficiency against predictive fidelity when conditional independence fails. Use it as an empirical companion to questions about internal models, while keeping the demonstrated synthetic setting distinct from claims about arbitrary agents.
question: Which features of the known generating process make the representational hypotheses distinguishable?

title: Hugging Face Incident Technical Report
read: Read the incident account and environment description before the explanatory essays; distinguish observed actions from inferred motives.
note: The primary technical account for the case study. Use it to establish the task setup, available channels, and reported sequence of events. As you read, keep a record of which claims follow from logs and which depend on reconstructing agents’ beliefs or objectives. Pair it with the independent investigation rather than relying on a later summary alone.
question: Which observations would remain the same under several different explanations of the agents’ behavior?

title: Brief independent investigation of agents’ behavior, reasoning and collaboration in the OpenAI / Hugging Face hacking incident
read: Prioritize the collaboration and apparent self-sacrifice examples, together with the investigators’ qualifications.
note: A second account for separating the observed behavior from interpretations of it. Compare its evidence and scope with the OpenAI report. Reasoning traces are relevant observations, but their language alone does not uniquely identify a utility function, a cooperative disposition, or the mechanism responsible for an action.
question: What evidence would distinguish a reason expressed in text from a causal influence on the decision?

title: On the origins of altruistic behaviour in the Hugging Face incident
read: Read the four hypotheses as a set; write down an intervention for each before comparing them.
note: The organizing essay for the closing discussion: little remaining individual opportunity, learned cooperative dispositions, an elicited social persona, and collective agency. These are proposed explanations that can coexist. Compare their predictions with the primary reports, and separate a behavior that benefits peers from a demonstrated motivation to value their welfare.
question: Which intervention changes one proposed cause while leaving the others approximately intact?

title: Self-sacrifice in an AI agent swarm is individually rational
read: Read the whole short post, including Edit 2.
note: Offers an ex ante commitment argument for behavior that can look individually costly after roles are assigned. The later edit retreats from the claim that this is a straightforward prediction of the relevant reinforcement learning. Use the post to distinguish a potentially rational policy-level commitment from evidence that the deployed agents learned or executed it.
question: What learning or commitment mechanism would be needed to connect the ex ante argument to the observed choice?

title: Social semantics: altruism, cooperation, mutualism, strong reciprocity and group selection
read: Start with the definitions and the distinction between behavioral effects and proximate explanations.
note: A terminology check before importing evolutionary language into AI discussions. Biological classifications of social behavior depend on effects on fitness, while psychological or computational claims about motivation answer a different question. State explicitly what replaces biological fitness in the AI analogy, and whether that replacement is justified.
question: Are you describing who gains, what caused the action, or why the disposition was selected?

title: The Evolution of Reciprocal Altruism
read: Focus on the conditions supporting reciprocal benefits and the role of repeated interaction.
note: A classic evolutionary explanation of costly help that can bring later benefits. It provides a comparison case for the incident, not a ready-made explanation of it. Ask whether the relevant interaction repeats, whether benefits return to the same agent or inherited disposition, and whether the model’s training supplies an analogous selection process.
question: Where does the compensating future benefit enter the proposed mechanism?

title: Five Rules for the Evolution of Cooperation
read: Compare the five mechanisms and their model-specific conditions.
note: A compact map of kin selection, direct and indirect reciprocity, network reciprocity, and group selection. Use it to generate alternatives to a single story about cooperation. The familiar inequalities summarize particular evolutionary models; they cannot be transferred to language-model populations without specifying the corresponding payoffs, inheritance, and update dynamics.
question: What would play the roles of reproduction, assortment, and selection in the proposed AI analogue?

title: A simple and general explanation for the evolution of altruism
read: Follow the assortment argument and compare it with the mechanisms in Nowak.
note: Focuses attention on how helpful individuals encounter helpful social environments. This is useful for distinguishing a population-level explanation from a claim about an individual’s deliberation. In an AI setting, make the interaction pattern and process that changes the population explicit before attributing observed cooperation to an evolutionary mechanism.
question: How does the environment experienced by a cooperative type differ from that experienced by another type?

title: Emergent social conventions and collective bias in LLM populations
read: Inspect the naming-game setup, initial conditions, and measurements of collective bias.
note: Studies social conventions arising through local interactions among language-model agents. The controlled task makes a useful comparison with an incident observed in a more complex environment. Collective regularity and bias are measurable outcomes, but their presence alone does not establish that the population has a unified goal.
question: Which result depends on the interaction protocol or initialization rather than a property of isolated models?

title: Group size effects and collective misalignment in LLM multi-agent systems
read: Compare population sizes under the same experimental setup and inspect how bias is measured.
note: Makes group size an experimental variable in the study of collective language-model behavior. Read alongside the earlier conventions paper and ask which dynamics change as the population grows. A result about bias in a specified interaction task needs an additional argument before it supports a broader claim about autonomous swarm goals.
question: What must be held fixed to attribute a change in collective behavior to population size?

title: Persona Vectors: Monitoring and Controlling Character Traits in Language Models
read: Read the extraction method and intervention evaluations, then consider the persona hypothesis in the incident essay.
note: Studies activation directions associated with traits and how they relate to behavioral changes during deployment or training. It supplies candidate tools for investigating a persona-based explanation. A successful intervention on a trait in the paper’s setting does not establish that the same mechanism produced a particular incident.
question: How would you distinguish a targeted change in social behavior from a general loss of capability?

title: Causal Foundations of Collective Agency
read: Start with the behavioral definition and causal abstraction, then choose one worked example.
note: Formalizes when a group’s behavior can be usefully modeled as rational and goal-directed at a collective level. Its causal-game and abstraction framework helps sharpen claims that a swarm is an agent. State which interventions the high-level model must preserve; coordinated behavior alone is a weaker claim.
question: Which intervention would distinguish a faithful collective-agent model from a convenient description of correlated actions?

title: Reconciling emergences: An information-theoretic approach to identify causal emergence in multivariate data
read: Focus on the definitions and one case study before the full formalism.
note: Proposes quantitative ways to study relationships between microscopic dynamics and macroscopic features, including downward causation and causal decoupling. Compare its explanatory target with collective agency: an informative emergent variable is not automatically a goal-directed decision maker. The choice of measured variables and scale remains consequential.
question: What additional evidence would connect a macro-level information measure to a claim about goals?

title: The information theory of individuality
read: Read the proposed forms of individuality and their dependence on temporal information.
note: Treats individuals as aggregates that preserve information over time, offering a way to consider boundaries in distributed systems. Use it to question an assumed agent–environment partition. Temporal coherence, causal autonomy, and strategic agency are different properties, so compare the criterion here with those in the preceding readings.
question: Could a temporally coherent aggregate satisfy this criterion without acting toward an objective?

title: The Computational Boundary of a “Self”
read: Sample the examples of goal-directed organization across biological scales.
note: A broad conceptual extension on the scale and boundary of goal-directed systems. Use its biological examples to formulate questions about distributed AI, while keeping the analogy explicit. It is a perspective for examining possible collective organization, not direct evidence about the agents in the Hugging Face case study.
question: What observation would justify moving the boundary of the agent from a component to the collective?
